CULTURE-CMT: Benchmarking Contextualized Social Media Translation

Linjuan Wu Affiliation: Xiaohongshu Inc. Email: wulinjuan@xiaohongshu.com    Dingming Li Affiliation: Xiaohongshu Inc. Affiliation: Zhejiang University    Yiwen Qiu Affiliation: Xiaohongshu Inc. Affiliation: Zhejiang University    Xinze Lyu Affiliation: Xiaohongshu Inc.    Ye Guo Affiliation: Xiaohongshu Inc.    Daoxin Zhang Affiliation: Xiaohongshu Inc.    Zhe Xu Affiliation: Xiaohongshu Inc.    Weiming Lu Affiliation: Zhejiang University
Abstract

Social-media comments are interactions, yet they are often translated and evaluated as isolated text. This mismatch is especially problematic when meaning depends on surrounding discussion, community-specific slang, or culturally situated expressions. We introduce CULTURE-CMT, a Chinese–English benchmark for contextualized social-media comment translation that restores the post and conversational context naturally available to users. Its 572 manually verified examples are organized into Slang, Context, and Both, enabling diagnostic analysis of distinct and interacting sources of translation difficulty. To support scalable evaluation, we further develop a retrieval-augmented cultural-effectiveness Judger that combines a calibrated scoring model with dynamically retrieved cultural knowledge. CULTURE-CMT reveals several non-trivial patterns. Providing interaction context improves most model configurations, but does not eliminate culturally ineffective translations. Examples requiring both contextual grounding and culturally situated language remain substantially more difficult than either source of difficulty alone. Moreover, larger models are not consistently better, and thinking produces highly model-dependent gains, including occasional degradation. In contrast, a 27B model adapted on benchmark-disjoint social-media data achieves the lowest observed invalidity rate among the evaluated configurations under thinking inference with context. Together, these results suggest that realistic social-media translation is not simply a matter of scaling models or reasoning longer, but of learning to translate meaning as it is constructed within evolving online interactions.

1 Introduction

Social media platforms are a critical deployment scenario for cross-lingual communication. Unlike formal genres such as news and encyclopedic writing, user-generated content (UGC) is rich in slang, community-specific expressions, and rapidly evolving non-standard forms (Baldwin et al., 2013; Michel and Neubig, 2018; Sun et al., 2024). Recent benchmarks have begun to study this setting systematically. CULTURE-MT (Wu et al., 2026) focuses on culturally grounded expressions and adaptation, while CSM-MTBench (Zhao et al., 2026) distinguishes longer, information-rich posts from short, reactive snippets. Related work further shows that slang, neologisms, tone, and other emerging online expressions remain challenging for strong LLMs (Mei et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025; Liang et al., 2025). Beyond these linguistic challenges, however, comments are interactions rather than isolated utterances: they respond to posts, add information, express stances, and often leave shared information implicit. Interactional context has been shown to help recover implicit emotion and sociopragmatic meaning (Lee and Lau, 2020; Zhang et al., 2023), while context-aware MT benchmarks diagnose discourse-level phenomena (Jwalapuram et al., 2020; Fernandes et al., 2023). Our focus is complementary: we preserve the native post–comment and parent–reply structure of social-media interactions and study it jointly with culturally situated language.

This interaction context can directly change how a comment should be understood and translated. As shown in Figure 1, consider the comment

除了紫薇其他人我都看，紫薇斗志全无 (“I can watch everyone except Ziwei. Ziwei has no fighting spirit.”). Without the surrounding discussion,

“紫薇” (“Ziwei”) is ambiguous and may naturally be associated with the well-known character from the Chinese television drama My Fair Princess. Given the surrounding discussion of the men’s round of 16 at the Rome Masters, however, it is correctly resolved as a community-specific nickname for Alexander Zverev. For platform users, such context is part of the information naturally available when reading the comment, rather than an additional hint. A small qualitative pilot over 15 randomly sampled comments further suggests that restoring post and conversational context can resolve some translation errors, but does not eliminate culturally ineffective outputs. Some failures instead involve slang or community-specific expressions, while context can occasionally lead models toward an incorrect interpretation. This raises a broader question: once the original interaction context is restored, what still limits social-media translation?

To study this question, we introduce CULTURE-CMT, a benchmark for contextualized machine translation that evaluates the cultural effectiveness of Chinese–English social-media comment translation. Each instance preserves the target comment together with its available post title, post content, and parent comment where applicable, covering both top-level comments and replies. Motivated by our preliminary observations and prior work on slang and emerging internet language (Wuraola et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025), we categorize examples into Slang, Context, and Both to analyze slang-related difficulty, contextual dependence, and their combination. We then use CULTURE-CMT as a stress test for three common routes to improving LLM-based translation: Scale, Reasoning, and Adaptation. This framing is motivated by recent evidence that specialized translation models can rival much larger general-purpose systems (Guo et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026), while explicit reasoning can benefit challenging interpretative language tasks (Wang et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2025).

Our results reveal a non-trivial pattern. Larger models are not consistently better, and thinking provides highly model-dependent gains. A 27B model adapted on benchmark-disjoint social-media data achieves the lowest observed invalidity rate among the evaluated configurations under thinking inference with context. Beyond aggregate performance, the difficulty breakdown shows that Both remains harder than Slang or Context alone among the analyzed models, highlighting the challenge of combining contextual grounding with culturally situated language. Together, these results suggest that progress in realistic social-media translation requires more than simply increasing model scale or reasoning compute.

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We introduce CULTURE-CMT, a Chinese–English social-media comment translation benchmark that preserves the interaction context naturally available to users.

  • •

    We provide a diagnostic evaluation framework that separates Slang, Context, and Both difficulties, together with a retrieval-augmented cultural-effectiveness Judger validated against human annotations.

  • •

    We compare Scale, Reasoning, and Adaptation, documenting non-monotonic scaling, model-dependent reasoning gains, and clear benefits from targeted adaptation of the same backbone.

2 Benchmark Construction

2.1 Task Definition

CULTURE-CMT evaluates Chinese–English social-media comment translation under the interaction context naturally available to users. Each instance contains a target comment cc and its available context, including the post title tt, post content pp, and, for replies, the parent comment rr. For a top-level comment, 𝒞={t,p}\mathcal{C}=\{t,p\}; for a reply, 𝒞={t,p,r}\mathcal{C}=\{t,p,r\}.

The task is to generate an English translation

y=f⁡(c,𝒞)y=f(c,\mathcal{C})

that preserves the intended meaning of cc in its original interaction context.

For diagnostic analysis, we categorize examples into three difficulty types: Slang, involving internet slang, abbreviations, community-specific expressions, or other culturally situated usages; Context, where interpretation depends on the surrounding interaction; and Both, where both sources of difficulty are present.

2.2 Construction Pipeline

CULTURE-CMT is constructed from naturally occurring social-media comments through a multi-stage pipeline (Figure 2). All source data were collected between April 12 and May 12, 2026. Starting from 40,000 comments with their original interaction context, the pipeline consists of candidate filtering, model-assisted annotation, difficulty verification, deduplication and balancing, and human review. The resulting benchmark contains 572 manually verified examples.

Candidate Filtering.

We first apply rule-based quality filters to malformed, overly short or long, template-like, and low-information comments. We then identify candidates containing either social-media-specific language, such as slang, abbreviations, and community-specific expressions, or potential contextual dependence. Candidates are required to have their original post context available. This stage yields approximately 10,000 examples.

Model-assisted Annotation.

We use GPT-5.5 to perform structured annotation over the candidate pool, including quality screening, difficulty type, topical domain, and the primary translation challenge. Approximately 5,000 examples are selected for subsequent verification. The annotation prompt and the 21 domain labels are provided in Appendix B.1 and Appendix B.5, respectively.

Difficulty Verification and Balancing.

We next verify translation difficulty using independently generated translations. Candidates are assessed for substantive semantic, cultural, slang-related, or contextual variation across translations. For Context and Both examples, we additionally compare translations generated with and without interaction context to confirm contextual dependence. Approximately 3,000 examples remain after verification.

We then apply character-level nn-gram deduplication and balance the candidate pool across the 21 topical domains and three difficulty types, resulting in 2,205 candidates for human review. The corresponding prompts are provided in Appendix B.2, Appendix B.3, and Appendix B.4.

Human Review.

Three graduate-student reviewers independently examine the 2,205 candidates, covering translation difficulty, difficulty-type validity, and context relevance, with cross-checking across reviewers. The review also includes screening for sensitive, inappropriate, private, and personally identifiable information. After human verification, 572 examples remain and constitute CULTURE-CMT.

2.3 Dataset Statistics

Figure 3 summarizes CULTURE-CMT along four dimensions: difficulty type, interaction structure, topical domain, and comment length.

The benchmark contains 207 Slang, 204 Context, and 161 Both examples, together with 301 top-level comments and 271 replies. Their interaction structures differ noticeably across difficulty types: Slang is dominated by top-level comments (157/207), whereas replies account for a larger share of Context (120/204) and Both (101/161). This pattern reflects the greater conversational dependence of the latter two categories.

CULTURE-CMT spans 21 social-media domains. The largest categories are Celebrities/Fandom (47), Games (46), and Film & TV (43), while the smallest domain still contains 14 examples, providing broad topical coverage across diverse social-media settings.

Target comments are concise overall but exhibit a long-tailed length distribution, with a median of 53 characters and a mean of 58.9. Available parent comments are shorter, with a median of 33 characters and a mean of 45.7. Together, these statistics reflect the short-form yet highly variable nature of social-media interaction.

3 Evaluation Protocol

CULTURE-CMT evaluates whether a translation preserves not only the literal meaning of a social-media comment, but also its culturally situated meaning, affect, and communicative intent. Following the cultural-effectiveness criterion of CULTURE-MT (Wu et al., 2026), each translation receives a four-level score

s∈{0,1,2,3},s\in\{0,1,2,3\},

where scores 0–1 indicate culturally ineffective translations and scores 2–3 indicate culturally effective ones. We adopt the CULTURE-MT scoring rubric, summarized together with our annotation procedure in Appendix E.2.

Our primary metric is the cultural invalidity rate (Invalid Rate),

Rinvalid=N0+N1N,R_{\mathrm{invalid}}=\frac{N_{0}+N_{1}}{N},

where NkN_{k} is the number of examples receiving score kk and N=572N=572 is the benchmark size. Missing translation outputs are assigned score 0. Lower values indicate better performance.

3.1 Cultural-effectiveness Judger

To support scalable evaluation, we train a Qwen3.5-27B cultural-effectiveness Judger (Figure 4). Its training corpus contains 200K source–translation pairs from public social-media data, balanced across the four score levels. Among them, 160K are labeled by Gemini 3.1 Pro and 40K are manually annotated under the CULTURE-MT criterion (Wu et al., 2026). The Judger training data are disjoint from the 40K source pool used to construct CULTURE-CMT. We additionally reserve development sets of 1,000–2,000 examples during training and a separate 432-pair human-annotated set for final Judger evaluation. Data separation details are provided in Appendix E.1.

Training proceeds in three stages. We first perform SFT on the 160K Gemini-labeled examples and then continue SFT on the 40K human-labeled examples. We subsequently initialize GRPO from the resulting checkpoint using 20K human-labeled examples, comprising 10K examples that remain challenging after SFT and 10K correctly judged examples. The GRPO reward combines accuracy and format objectives: correct binary and four-way judgments receive rewards of 1 and 0.5, respectively, while the format reward encourages analysis followed by a final score. Training uses Relax (Relax Contributors, 2026); full configurations are provided in Appendix E.3.

The resulting Judger predicts

s^=fθ​(x,𝒞,y),\hat{s}=f_{\theta}(x,\mathcal{C},y),

where xx is the source comment, 𝒞\mathcal{C} is its interaction context, and yy is the candidate translation.

3.2 Agent-enhanced Judger

Social-media evaluation frequently requires knowledge of rapidly evolving slang, memes, fandom terminology, named entities, and platform-specific expressions. We therefore augment the trained Judger with a retrieval agent that supplies relevant cultural knowledge at inference time.

Given (x,𝒞,y)(x,\mathcal{C},y), the evaluation process is

Q\displaystyle Q =gplan​(x,𝒞,y),\displaystyle=g_{\mathrm{plan}}(x,\mathcal{C},y),
D\displaystyle D =R⁡(Q),\displaystyle=R(Q),
H\displaystyle H =ghint​(x,𝒞,y,Q,D),\displaystyle=g_{\mathrm{hint}}(x,\mathcal{C},y,Q,D),
s^\displaystyle\hat{s} =fθ​(x,𝒞,y,H),\displaystyle=f_{\theta}(x,\mathcal{C},y,H),

where gplang_{\mathrm{plan}} identifies knowledge needed for evaluation and generates search queries, RR retrieves relevant evidence, and ghintg_{\mathrm{hint}} converts the evidence into concise, translation-specific judging hints.

Retrieved evidence serves as auxiliary knowledge for the calibrated Judger, which produces the final 0–3 cultural-effectiveness score. This design combines a learned evaluation criterion with dynamically retrieved cultural information, allowing the evaluator to accommodate emerging social-media usages at inference time. Full agent prompts are provided in Appendix C.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Models.

We evaluate 33 model configurations spanning multiple families and scales, including Qwen3.5-9B, 27B and 35B-A3B (Team, 2026), Qwen3.6-27B(Google, 2026c), Qwen3.8-27B and Qwen3.8-Max (Qwen Team, 2026), GLM-5.2 and GLM-5.3 (GLM-5-Team et al., 2026), Gemini 3.1 Pro (Google, 2026a) and Gemini 3.7 Flash (Google, 2026b), Gemma-4-31B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B (Team et al., 2026a), Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic, 2026), GPT-5.6 (OpenAI, 2026), and Kimi K3 (Team et al., 2026b). Where both inference modes are available, we evaluate thinking and non-thinking configurations of the same model. Cross-model results are interpreted descriptively, as model families differ in architecture and training, while thinking and non-thinking configurations use their native inference settings.

We also evaluate Qwen3.6-27B-SFT, a 27B model adapted for social-media translation using 1.2M training examples strictly disjoint from CULTURE-CMT. This provides a task-adapted comparison alongside the general-purpose models. Details of data construction and supervised fine-tuning are provided in Appendix D.

Evaluation.

We follow the cultural-effectiveness evaluation protocol described in Section 3. Our primary metric is the proportion of translations receiving scores 0 or 1, denoted as the Invalid Rate; lower values indicate better cultural effectiveness. We additionally report the proportion of score-3 translations and the mean score. Judger inference uses greedy decoding (temperature 0). Contextualized and comment-only translations are evaluated with their corresponding with-context and without-context Judger prompts, so each condition reflects the complete translation-and-evaluation setting available under that context regime.

4.2 Evaluation of the Cultural-effectiveness Judger

We assess the Judger against human annotations on translations of final CULTURE-CMT examples.

Data and Metrics.

For each of the 33 model configurations, we sample 25 source–translation pairs: 5 Slang, 10 Context, and 10 Both, yielding 825 candidates. After human annotation, we sample by the adjudicated 0–3 labels to construct an approximately score-balanced 432-pair evaluation set. This set is reserved for final Judger evaluation. Appendix E.2 describes the double-annotation and adjudication procedure.

We report binary accuracy and Cohen’s κ\kappa for the ineffective/effective partition ({0,1}\{0,1\} versus {2,3}\{2,3\}), together with four-way accuracy and Spearman’s ρ\rho over the original scores. The balanced evaluation set enables comparison across evaluators under comparable score coverage.

Results.

The combined agent enhancement increases observed binary accuracy by 1.16 and 4.17 percentage points for the SFT and GRPO-aligned Judgers, respectively, while improving all four reported metrics for both backbones (Figure 5). GRPO alone improves ordinal agreement (ρ\rho: 0.5889 to 0.6131), but reduces binary and four-way accuracy. The Agent Judger with the GRPO-aligned backbone achieves the highest binary accuracy (77.31%), κ\kappa (0.5498), and ρ\rho (0.6554), whereas the SFT-based Agent Judger slightly leads in four-way accuracy. The main translation experiments use the GRPO-based Agent Judger. Its agreement with humans is assessed on the separate 432-pair evaluation set described above.

4.3 Overall Results and Difficulty Profiles

Table 1 summarizes the complete score distributions under both contextualized and comment-only settings. We report the proportions of scores 0–3, the cultural invalidity rate (Invalid↓\downarrow, i.e., scores 0 and 1), and the mean score. To quantify the effect of interaction context, we define

ΔInvalid=RInvalidno-ctx−RInvalidctx,ΔMean=μctx−μno-ctx,\Delta_{\text{Invalid}}=R_{\text{Invalid}}^{\text{no-ctx}}-R_{\text{Invalid}}^{\text{ctx}},\qquad\Delta_{\text{Mean}}=\mu^{\text{ctx}}-\mu^{\text{no-ctx}},

where positive values indicate better scores in the contextualized condition. Translation and Judger prompts both change between conditions. Within each inference mode, models are ordered by contextualized Invalid↓\downarrow.

Effect of Interaction Context.

Most configurations achieve lower Invalid Rates and higher mean scores when interaction context is available, although the magnitude of the improvement varies substantially across models. For example, non-thinking GLM-5.2 improves from 30.1% to 21.7% Invalid, while thinking GPT-5.6 Terra improves by 8.7 percentage points. By contrast, thinking Gemini 3.1 Pro has the same Invalid Rate in both settings, with only a small increase in mean score. These results show that interaction context is broadly useful, but models differ considerably in how effectively they exploit it.

4.4 Difficulty Profiles under Thinking Inference

We next describe difficulty profiles for the evaluated thinking configurations with context.

Figure 6 shows Invalid rates on the Slang, Context, and Both subsets for representative models. Across the models shown, Both is consistently the most challenging subset. Even systems that perform relatively well on Slang or Context individually often exhibit substantially higher Invalid rates on Both, indicating that the combination of contextual dependence and socially situated language remains difficult. For example, Qwen3.6-27B-SFT has an Invalid Rate of 26.7% on Both, compared with 15.9% on Slang and 12.3% on Context. GLM-5.2 shows a similar profile, with 17.9%, 12.7%, and 26.7% on the three subsets, respectively.

The figure also shows that similar overall performance can mask different difficulty profiles. Some models are relatively stronger on Context but weaker on Slang, while others show the opposite tendency. For instance, Qwen3.5-27B performs competitively on Context (14.2%) but remains much weaker on Both (28.0%). By contrast, Kimi K3 exhibits a more balanced profile across the three subsets. The three-way partition thus makes model-specific difficulty profiles visible beyond a single aggregate score.

Our adapted Qwen3.6-27B-SFT has its lowest Invalid Rate on Context, while its higher error rate on Both identifies the combined difficulty as a remaining challenge under thinking inference.

4.5 Scale, Reasoning, and Adaptation

We next compare three common routes for improving LLM-based social-media translation: Scale, Reasoning, and Adaptation. Figure 7 summarizes their performance under the contextualized setting.

Scale.

Within Qwen3.5 under thinking inference, Invalid decreases from 29.7% at 9B to 18.9% at 27B, while the 122B-A10B and 397B variants obtain 20.8% and 21.3%. The observed ranking is therefore non-monotonic in total parameter count. For mixture-of-experts models, total and active parameter counts also differ.

Reasoning.

Thinking inference lowers Invalid by 15.0, 12.6, and 11.5 percentage points for Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, and Qwen3.6-27B, respectively. Claude Opus 5, Qwen3.8-27B, and Qwen3.8-Max instead have higher Invalid Rates under thinking inference. The benefit of switching to thinking mode therefore varies across models.

Adaptation.

SFT of the same Qwen3.6-27B backbone lowers Invalid from 34.6% to 24.8% without thinking and from 23.1% to 17.7% with thinking. The adapted model achieves the lowest observed contextualized Invalid Rate among the evaluated configurations.

Scope.

CULTURE-CMT is a targeted stress test constructed from social-media data collected between April 12 and May 12, 2026. Accordingly, our results characterize the evaluated benchmark and model configurations rather than population-level platform error rates. The scale and reasoning analyses are descriptive comparisons across existing configurations, while the adaptation comparison captures the full effect of the proposed SFT procedure.

5 Conclusion

We introduced CULTURE-CMT, a 572-example benchmark for Chinese–English social-media comment translation that preserves the post and conversational context naturally available to users. The benchmark supports diagnostic analysis through its Slang, Context, and Both subsets under the cultural-effectiveness rubric inherited from CULTURE-MT. We further develop a Qwen3.5-27B cultural-effectiveness Judger augmented with retrieved cultural information and evaluate its agreement with human annotations. Across the evaluated configurations, interaction context generally improves cultural effectiveness, while the Both subset remains the most challenging among the models analyzed. Performance is non-monotonic across model sizes, the benefit of thinking varies substantially by model, and targeted adaptation of the same 27B backbone lowers Invalid Rates in both inference modes. Overall, these findings highlight the importance of jointly modeling interaction context and culturally situated language, and suggest targeted adaptation as a promising direction for improving social-media translation.

AI Use Statement

We used generative AI tools to assist with manuscript organization and grammatical editing, as well as figure preparation and consistency checks during revision. The model-assisted data screening, annotation, translation generation and refinement, and reasoning-trace generation used in this study are described in Section 2.2, Section 3.1, and Appendix D. The authors manually reviewed the AI-assisted revisions for correctness and consistency with the reported results and take full responsibility for the final content, including the text, figures, analyses, and conclusions.

Appendix A Related Work

A.1 Social Media and Culturally Grounded Translation

Machine translation for social-media text has long been recognized as challenging because of its noisy, informal, and rapidly evolving nature. One challenge is robustness to linguistic noise, which MTNT (Michel and Neubig, 2018) studies through naturally occurring Reddit comments. A complementary challenge is that translations must preserve not only understandable content, but also community-specific meanings, tone, and expressive style. RedTrans (Guo et al., 2025) addresses this through specialized training for social-media translation, while CULTURE-MT (Wu et al., 2026) evaluates cultural effectiveness through expression accuracy and cultural adaptability. CSM-MTBench (Zhao et al., 2026) further distinguishes longer posts from short, reactive comments, highlighting difficulties in preserving slang, tone, and style. Related studies examine slang interpretation and cross-cultural nuances more directly (Sun et al., 2024; Wuraola et al., 2024). Studies of emerging slang and internet buzzwords further examine how contextual usage helps interpret unfamiliar expressions (Mei et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025).

CULTURE-CMT complements these efforts by evaluating translation within the original interaction in which a comment occurs. It retains the corresponding post and parent comment where available, preserving the contextual information naturally accessible to readers. The Slang, Context, and Both subsets additionally support separate analyses of linguistic-cultural difficulty, contextual dependence, and their combination.

A.2 Context-aware and Discourse-level Translation

DiP diagnoses anaphora, lexical consistency, coherence/readability, and discourse connectives in machine translation (Jwalapuram et al., 2020). MuDA uses a data-driven procedure to identify translation phenomena requiring context and supports multilingual discourse evaluation (Fernandes et al., 2023). CULTURE-CMT complements this line of work by retaining explicit post and parent-comment fields and selecting culturally situated comment-translation challenges. Its contribution is the combination of interaction structure, difficulty-based selection, three diagnostic subsets, and cultural-effectiveness evaluation, rather than the introduction of context into MT evaluation.

A.3 Scale, Reasoning, and Adaptation for Translation

Large-scale multilingual training has advanced machine translation (NLLB Team et al., 2022), while specialized systems demonstrate the potential of more compact models. Seed-X (Cheng et al., 2025) develops 7B multilingual translation models, and Hy-MT2 (Zheng et al., 2026) similarly targets efficient translation in real-world settings. RedTrans (Guo et al., 2025) explores domain-specific training for social-media translation, while SlangDIT (Liang et al., 2025) investigates reasoning-based interpretative slang translation.

We bring these directions into a shared evaluation setting to examine Scale, Reasoning, and Adaptation. Specifically, we compare models across sizes, evaluate thinking and non-thinking modes within the same model where available, and include a social-media translation model fine-tuned on benchmark-disjoint data. The contribution is a descriptive assessment under a common cultural-effectiveness criterion, rather than a controlled decomposition of the three strategies. Our model coverage does not include Seed-X or Hy-MT2. Prior CULTURE-MT results place the evaluated Seed-X variants below Qwen3-32B on cultural effectiveness (Wu et al., 2026), motivating our focus on Qwen-family baselines; this earlier result does not establish their relative performance on CULTURE-CMT. The omission of specialized MT systems limits the scope of the comparison.

Appendix B Prompts for Benchmark Construction

This appendix provides the prompts used in the construction of CULTURE-CMT. All prompts operate on the original Chinese social-media content. For clarity, we present the prompts in English while preserving the exact task definitions and output formats used in our pipeline.

B.1 Model-assisted Candidate Annotation

After rule-based candidate mining, we use an LLM to determine whether each candidate contains a genuine translation challenge and to assign its difficulty type. The model is given the target comment together with its original interaction context.

B.2 Independent Translation Generation

For candidates that pass the annotation stage, we generate independent translations for difficulty verification. The translation model receives the target comment and, when required by the experimental condition, its interaction context.

For the comment-only condition used in context-dependence verification, the same instruction is used but the post and parent-comment fields are omitted.

B.3 Translation Difficulty Verification

Model-assisted annotation may retain examples that appear unusual but do not produce substantial translation difficulty. We therefore generate two translations independently and ask a verifier to determine whether their differences reflect a genuine translation challenge or only stylistic variation.

B.4 Context-dependence Verification

For candidates labeled as Context or Both, we perform an additional verification step to ensure that the interaction context is genuinely necessary for recovering the intended meaning.

For the same target comment, we generate one translation using the target comment alone and another using the full interaction context. A verifier then determines whether access to context leads to a substantive improvement or change in interpretation.

B.5 Domain Labels

We use 21 topical domains for annotation and balancing: Games; Anime / ACG; Film and Television; Celebrities / Fandom; Music; Relationships / Dating; Psychology / Personality Tests; Food; Fashion / Beauty; Fitness / Exercise; Sports; Travel; Housing / Home; Careers / Job Seeking; Education / Learning; Parenting / Family; Pets; Drawing / Handcraft; Technology / Automotive; Finance / Investment; and Daily Life / Other.

Appendix C Agent-enhanced Judger Prompts

This appendix provides the prompts used by the retrieval component of the Agent-enhanced Judger described in Section 3.2. The retrieval module supplies auxiliary cultural knowledge when necessary, while the trained cultural-effectiveness Judger retains final scoring authority. All prompts are presented in English for readability.

C.1 Search Planning Prompt

The search planner determines whether external knowledge is required to evaluate a candidate translation and generates a small number of searchable queries when necessary.

C.2 Hint Generation Prompt

The hint generator converts retrieved information into concise, translation-specific judging points. It does not assign the final cultural-effectiveness score.

C.3 Hint Injection Template

The structured hint object is serialized into an auxiliary block and inserted into the Judger input. The prompt explicitly instructs the Judger to treat the hints as supplementary evidence rather than authoritative labels.

Appendix D Social-Media Translation Fine-Tuning

Data Collection and Refinement.

We collect 1.5M Chinese comments from public social-media platforms between April 12 and May 12, 2026, together with their available post and parent-comment context. Following the data-distillation and refinement approach of CULTURE-MT (Wu et al., 2026), we use Gemini to generate English translations and a static cultural-effectiveness Judger to assess their quality. Translations requiring improvement are refined by Gemini using Judger feedback. After filtering and refinement, we retain 1.2M contextualized source–translation examples, strictly disjoint from CULTURE-CMT. The translation-generation prompts are provided below.

Thinking and Non-thinking Supervision.

For each retained sample, GLM-5 generates a concise reasoning trace consisting of context analysis and translation points. The context analysis summarizes the information relevant to interpreting the comment, while the translation points identify key expressions and explain their translation considerations. This task-specific supervision encourages attention to contextual and cultural challenges without unnecessarily long reasoning. The reasoning-generation prompt is provided below.

We organize the retained data into an equal mixture of thinking and non-thinking supervision, with 600K examples in each subset. Thinking examples include the generated reasoning trace followed by the final English translation, whereas non-thinking examples retain only the final translation as the supervision target. Both subsets are combined to train a single model that supports evaluation in either inference mode.

Training Configuration.

We train Qwen3.6-27B-SFT on the combined 1.2M-example dataset using the Relax framework (Relax Contributors, 2026). Training runs for one epoch with a global batch size of 256 and a learning rate of 5×10−65\times 10^{-6}. Development validation examples are separated from the training collection, as described in Appendix E.1.

Appendix E Data Separation, Annotation, and Judger Configuration

E.1 Data provenance and separation

All source collections in this study were gathered between April 12 and May 12, 2026. The 40K benchmark source comments and the 200K Judger source–translation pairs are disjoint collections gathered during the same period; they do not constitute a temporal train–test split. The 1.2M retained translation-training examples are disjoint from the final CULTURE-CMT benchmark. Development validation sets contain 1,000–2,000 examples held out from the corresponding training collections. These development sets are separate from the 432-pair final human evaluation of Judger outputs. The latter consists of multi-model translations of final benchmark examples and is not used for training, validation during training, checkpoint selection, or evaluator selection.

The static Judger used for translation-data refinement and the agent-enhanced evaluator follow the same cultural-effectiveness criterion. Their shared criterion is part of the training/evaluation design, not evidence of independent human confirmation of the adapted model’s ranking. The reported collection-level separation does not by itself establish that all related posts, threads, or recurring expressions are independent across collections.

E.2 Human annotation and scoring rubric

Nine Chinese–English bilingual experts annotate translation quality in both the training and evaluation collections. Each batch is annotated twice. In each round, its examples are divided equally among three experts, so each example receives one label per round, not three votes. The two rounds use six different experts; assignments are randomized across batches rather than fixed throughout the project. After both rounds, the remaining three experts adjudicate disagreements and determine the final labels. The mean binary agreement between the two rounds is 82.46%, with labels 0–1 mapped to ineffective and labels 2–3 to effective. This is an agreement statistic for the two annotation rounds, not nine-way agreement or four-class exact agreement.

Benchmark candidate review is a separate task: three additional graduate students divide the 2,205 candidates equally, review difficulty and context relevance, and cross-check their work. The resulting 572 examples form the benchmark. For final Judger evaluation, 25 pairs are sampled from each of 33 model configurations (5 Slang, 10 Context, and 10 Both), giving 825 candidate pairs. Human annotation precedes subsampling by adjudicated score to obtain the approximately balanced 432-pair set.

We reuse the four-level CULTURE-MT rubric without changing its definitions (Wu et al., 2026). Its two dimensions concern fidelity to meaning and affect, and appropriate cultural interpretation and natural target-language expression. The following is a concise summary, not a new scoring scale:

  • •

    0: Major failure to convey the intended meaning or cultural intent.

  • •

    1: Some meaning is understandable, but cultural communication remains ineffective.

  • •

    2: Communication is generally effective, with residual weaknesses in style or cultural expression.

  • •

    3: Meaning, affect, and culturally situated intent are conveyed effectively and naturally.

The effective/ineffective boundary remains between scores 1 and 2. The Gemini judging setup follows CULTURE-MT’s protocol, with Gemini 3.1 Pro used in this study and the context input matched to the evaluation condition.

E.3 Judger training and inference

All trained Judgers use Qwen3.5-27B. GRPO starts from the Judger checkpoint obtained after the two SFT stages, and uses the Relax framework (Relax Contributors, 2026) with a Megatron training backend and SGLang rollouts. The Judger’s GRPO training reward is

r=raccuracy+rformat.r=r_{\mathrm{accuracy}}+r_{\mathrm{format}}.

The accuracy component rewards agreement with the annotated score: 1 for a correct ineffective/effective decision and 0.5 for a correct four-level score. The format component rewards an analysis followed by the final score. The configuration below records the supplied GRPO launch settings; it does not describe the separate translation SFT run.

Disabling the chat template’s built-in thinking mode is distinct from the task’s required analysis-before-score output format. Final Judger scoring uses temperature 0. The training rollout temperature of 0.9 applies only to generating GRPO samples. Contextualized translations use the with-context Judger prompt; comment-only translations use the without-context prompt. The agent planning and hint templates are given in Appendix C.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
